title: Template‑Driven Validation & Error Messages ❌
description: Show validation feedback using control state and template references.

slides.title: Built‑In HTML5 Validators ➕
slides.content:
# Angular respects native validation attributes

Add `required`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `pattern`, etc., directly to your inputs. Angular will hook into them.

```html
<input name="username" [(ngModel)]="username" required minlength="3" maxlength="20">
```

Angular tracks the control’s validity in `control.valid`, `control.invalid`, and the specific errors object.

slides.title: Accessing a Control's State
slides.content: Use a template reference on the ngModel directive: `#usernameRef="ngModel"`
slides.codeSnippet: Username is required. Must be at least 3 characters.

quizData.question: Which property on a control reference tells if the user has interacted with the field and then left it?
quizData.explanation: `touched` becomes `true` when the field loses focus after being visited. `dirty` means the value was changed.

slides.title: Important Control States 📊
slides.content:
Every `ngModel` control tracks:

* `valid` / `invalid` – overall validity.
* `pristine` / `dirty` – has the user modified the value?
* `touched` / `untouched` – has the field been focused?
* `errors` – an object with validation error names (e.g., `{ required: true }`).

Use these to show/hide error messages at the right time – usually after the field is `touched` and `invalid`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Show Errors Only After Interaction

It’s a better UX to show errors after the field loses focus (touched) rather than on page load. Use `*ngIf="control.invalid && control.touched"`.

quizData.question: You should always show validation errors as soon as the page loads.
quizData.explanation: It’s best to delay error display until the user has interacted with the field (touched or dirty).
